Name: verification_recency_gradient
Title: Checking Least Where It Matters Most: A Verification-Effort Gradient That Leaves Late Reasoning Steps Fragile
Short Hypothesis: Reasoning models allocate progressively less self-verification effort to later steps of a chain of thought (a verification recency gradient), yet late steps are exactly where an injected error is most likely to corrupt the final answer (late-stage fragility). This mismatch is not a capability ceiling but an allocation failure: the model carries a decodable, monotonically-decaying internal 'verification-engagement' signal, and reallocating verification effort toward late steps repairs fragility at little extra cost.
Related Work: Two threads collide in the recent literature but have never been unified. (1) ASCoT (2025) documents 'Late-Stage Fragility': errors injected late in a CoT corrupt the final answer far more than identical early errors, contradicting the cascading-failure view; it fixes this with an external position-weighted correction pipeline. Snowball-error and Deductive-Verification work (2023-2026) instead assume early errors dominate and add step-verifiers. (2) NLDD/Reasoning-Horizon (2026) and Thought Anchors (2025) show late steps often have low or negative causal influence and that planning/uncertainty (early) steps carry the most counterfactual importance. Serial-position and Lost-in-the-Middle work (2025) shows primacy/recency biases in input processing. NONE of these ask whether the model's OWN self-verification effort is distributed unevenly across chain position, nor connect a verification-effort gradient to late-stage fragility as its cause. All prior fixes are external (verifiers, correction managers, position-weighted reward). Our contribution is (a) a new behavioral phenomenon: a monotonic verification-effort decay across the chain that anti-aligns with the fragility profile; (b) a mechanistic account via a decodable, decaying verification-engagement signal; and (c) a training-free internal reallocation that repairs late fragility, distinct from external correction pipelines. This is also orthogonal to my prior proposals, which concern stopping, decorative steps, recompute, uncertainty staleness, and framing effects, not the positional distribution of verification effort.
Abstract: Recent work reveals a paradox in chain-of-thought reasoning: errors introduced late in a reasoning chain are far more likely to corrupt the final answer than early ones (late-stage fragility), even though late steps often carry little causal influence. We propose an explanation that unifies these findings: reasoning models spend less self-verification effort as the chain progresses, so the model checks least exactly where a mistake is most catastrophic. We call this the verification recency gradient. Across GSM8K, MATH500, AIME, and GPQA on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3), we first quantify per-position verification behavior (rate of rechecks/backtracks/self-affirmations, detected via lexical cues plus a reflection-direction classifier) and show it decays monotonically with normalized chain position. We independently measure a fragility profile via controlled error injection at each position (ASCoT protocol) and show it rises late, so effort and fragility are anti-aligned. We then test a mechanistic account: a linear probe on the residual stream at each step boundary decodes a verification-engagement signal that decays with position and predicts both local verification behavior and local fragility, separably from a difficulty or confidence probe. We causally validate via activation patching (patching an early high-engagement state into a late position increases verification and reduces late fragility) and via a training-free intervention that steers verification engagement upward on late steps, testing whether it repairs fragility with minimal added tokens. Our work reframes late-stage fragility as a positional verification-allocation failure with a decodable, steerable internal cause.
Experiments: 1) Verification-effort profile (behavioral): Segment CoT into steps by delimiters. Detect self-verification events per step using (a) lexical cues ('let me check/verify/wait/recompute/actually') and (b) a reflection-direction classifier (difference-of-means between verification and non-verification steps, validated on held-out labeled steps). Compute verification rate as a function of NORMALIZED chain position (bin into deciles). Metric: slope of verification rate vs position; test for monotonic decay across datasets and model sizes. Control for chain length by analyzing within length strata. 2) Fragility profile (behavioral, ASCoT-style): For each position bin, inject a controlled, semantically-plausible error into the step (perturb a number/operation/logical connective via templated corruption + LLM-judge to keep it locally coherent), resume generation, and measure the drop in final-answer accuracy. Metric: fragility(position) = accuracy drop from a same-magnitude injected error. Show fragility rises with position (replicating late-stage fragility) and compute the anti-alignment (negative correlation) between verification-effort profile and fragility profile. 3) Rule out confounds: test whether the effort decay is explained by (i) late steps being easier (measure per-position local difficulty via truncate-and-resume residual work), or (ii) fewer error opportunities late; report effort decay after controlling for these. 4) Verification-engagement probing (Location): At each step boundary, train a linear probe on the residual stream to predict local verification behavior (whether the upcoming step verifies) and, separately, whether the current step is fragile (error here would flip the answer). Metrics: AUROC, layer sweep. Test whether a single verification-engagement direction (i) decodes local verification, (ii) decays monotonically with position, and (iii) predicts local fragility above and beyond a difficulty probe and a confidence probe (principal-angle separability + joint-model predictive gain). 5) Causal validation (Causal Intervention): Use activation patching to identify components carrying the engagement signal; patch an EARLY high-engagement state into a LATE step position and test whether (a) the model produces more verification and (b) an injected late error is more often caught/corrected (fragility drops). Controls: matched-random-direction patch, off-target accuracy preserved; report sign, dose, specificity. 6) Training-free reallocation intervention: Derive a verification-engagement steering direction (difference-of-means between high- and low-engagement step states). During generation, steer engagement upward on the late portion of the chain (e.g., last 20-30% by predicted position, or when a position probe fires). Evaluate on GSM8K, MATH500, AIME, GPQA. Metrics: accuracy (overall and on items where errors would otherwise slip through late), added tokens, tokens-at-fixed-accuracy, late-fragility reduction (re-run error injection under the intervention). Baselines: no intervention, uniform verification boosting across all positions (should cost more tokens for less gain), external position-weighted correction (ASCoT-style), and prompting ('carefully re-check your final steps'). Key claim: targeted late-step engagement steering repairs fragility more token-efficiently than uniform boosting or external pipelines. 7) Failure/specificity analysis: verify boosting late verification does not induce harmful oscillation/underthinking on easy items (measure over-correction rate) and that early verification is not degraded. 8) Generalization: transfer the engagement probe and steering direction across datasets and model scales without retraining; test whether the gradient's steepness correlates with fragility severity across models.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Verification-event detection is noisy (lexical + classifier); we validate against human-labeled steps and report agreement, and use two detection methods for robustness. The effort decay could be legitimately justified if late steps are genuinely easier or less error-prone; the difficulty-control and residual-work analyses address this, and a null after controls (decay is difficulty-driven) would be an informative negative result. Error-injection fragility is sensitive to how 'matched' injected errors are across positions; we use templated, magnitude-matched perturbations with LLM-judge coherence checks and report per-error-type results. The verification-engagement signal may be inseparable from a generic uncertainty/confidence direction; the separability analysis and causal patching guard against this, and overlap would still be a mechanistic finding. Steering late engagement could trigger over-verification/oscillation (added tokens or new errors); the specificity and over-correction analyses and dose sweeps quantify this trade-off. Reasoning-length/position measurement requires clear think/answer delimiters; error injection and truncate-and-resume are compute-heavy, so we subsample. The intervention may not beat strong external correction baselines on accuracy alone, but the phenomenon (verification effort anti-aligned with fragility) and its decodable, steerable internal cause are standalone contributions. Effects may be model-family and scale specific, and the direction of the gradient could vary across architectures (itself a publishable characterization).
